claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature compressive ductility.
Approximately 20 at.% Mo should be replaced with Ta.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at about 1200 °C for 24 hours will produce a uniform, single-phase disordered BCC structure in the modified alloy.
Replacing Mo with Ta will reduce the alloy's average electronegativity difference.
Replacing Mo with Ta will moderate local lattice-distortion fields.
Reducing Mo concentration will lessen local lattice strain and dislocation pinning.
Reduced lattice strain and dislocation pinning will facilitate dislocation motion during room-temperature compression.
The modified alloy will retain sufficient solid-solution strengthening despite the reduction in Mo.
The modified alloy will retain a room-temperature compressive yield strength near 1700 MPa.
The modified alloy will exhibit a roughly 20–30% increase in room-temperature plastic strain relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength–plasticity effect is limited to a narrow substitution range around 20 at.% Ta replacing Mo.
Substitution outside that narrow range may cause phase instability or adverse mechanical-property changes.
The proposed mechanism is supported by analogous refractory high-entropy alloy systems.
The magnitude of ductility improvement and retention of yield strength may depend on processing and microstructural evolution.

contradictions.description: The change is called a partial substitution, but the equiatomic five-component baseline contains 20 at.% Mo, so replacing approximately 20 atomic percentage points of Mo would remove essentially all Mo. If instead the intent is to replace 20% of the Mo inventory, the modified alloy would contain about 4 at.% Ta and 16 at.% Mo. The proposed composition is therefore internally ambiguous.
